newsitem.title: DUBAI: Saudi bank launches fund, opens doors to foreigners.
newsitem.headline: Saudi bank launches fund, opens doors to foreigners.

text.p: Saudi American Bank (SAMBA) on Monday launched Saudi Arabia's first fund to allow foreign participation in the Gulf's biggest bourse, marking the slow opening of doors to international investors in the kingdom.

SAMBA, 30 percent owned by Citibank , had in March received Saudi central bank approval to set up the Saudi Arabia Investment Fund Ltd (SAIF) in which foreigners can own units in the Saudi market, so far limited to Saudis and other Gulf Arabs.

"SAMBA announces the launch of the Saudi Arabia Investment Fund Limited (SAIF), a new investment company that will for the first time allow international portfolio investors access to Saudi Arabian equity securities," a bank statement said.
"SAIF represents the first opportunity for persons who are not Saudi Arabian nationals to have unrestricted access to securities quoted on the Saudi Stock market," it added.
It did not say what the capital of the fund would be.
Bankers said SAMBA is aiming to raise up to $200 million in the closed-end fund which will be listed on the London Stock Exchange, with minimum subscription at $20,000 at $10 a share.
Subscription would end by the end of July, they added.
The statement said ING Baring Securities Limited was the fund's international placing agent and SAMBA the placing agent in Saudi Arabia, the world's largest oil exporter and producer.
"The shares are being marketed to institutions in Europe, the Far East and the Middle East," it said.

Bankers said the move will usher in similar funds, for which some banks are awaiting central bank approval. But they cautioned that although the fund showed the kingdom was slowly opening its doors to international investors, a more significant foreign role was still some way off.
Only Saudi nationals can hold shares in all of the over 70 local firms, capitalised at some $45 billion, listed in Riyadh.

Nationals of the other five Gulf Arab states can own Saudi equities, excluding banks -- which account for about a third of market capitalisation -- and certain other stocks. Analysts said Riyadh was likely to follow the example of markets in Asia, which have gradually allowed foreigners in.

Foreign participation could stem the flow of billions of dollars remitted every year by the six million expatriates in the kingdom and improve liquidity. It could also lure back some of the $100 billion in Saudi private wealth estimated to be offshore, analysts said.

It will also help boost the private sector in the kigndom where the government is trying to diversify from reliance on oil earnings and urging a biggger private sector role in the economy, they added.

Official data show 137.8 million shares worth 25.4 billion riyals ($6.8 billion) were traded last year. This compares to 25.7 billion shares worth $19.3 billion in nearby Kuwait, where at $22 billion, market capitalisation is half that of Riyadh.

Saudi Arabia is behind some of its neighbours in opening up. Oman already allows 49 percent foreign ownership and in Bahrain, foreigners resident in the country for at least two years are allowed limited investment in most listed firms.
Shares are currently dealt by computer and telephone in trading rooms in banks across the kingdom.

Saudi Finance Minister Ibrahim Abdel Aziz al-Asaf said in May the kingdom was reviewing its bourse, including possible measures to further invite foreign and Gulf Arab investors, including gradually opening up the bourse to international investors though further equity funds.
"We are moving in the direction of openness, but at the same time we want to make sure we will do it the right way," he said.
